title: SYSK Distraction Playlist: SYSK Live: How Bars Work
summary: A live recording of Stuff You Should Know (Vancouver stop) from the Distraction Playlist, covering the history of bars and bartending. The hosts trace bars from ancient Pompeii hot snack bars and Roman road inns, through Shawn's in Athlone, Ireland, and Vancouver's Gassy Jack and the Globe bar, to the US Pioneer Inn and Tavern law of 1832, 19th-century election-day "swilling" with bumbo, and the first celebrity bartender Erasmus Willard. They profile Jerry Thomas (Blue Blazer, 1862 bartender's guide), then cover Prohibition and speakeasies, Canadian doctor-prescribed liquor, the 1970s fern bar era (Henry Africa's, Perry's), Dale DeGroff's revival of classic cocktails, and cocktail origins (sling, sour, daisy, margarita, martini, daiquiri, Tom Collins, mojito, Caesar). The episode closes with Canadian whiskey and the Canadian Club "Hide a Case" campaign. Sponsor read for Squarespace in the middle.

segments.title: Opening banter and bar origins question
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter and ask whether listeners realize bars are one of the oldest businesses, noting that alcohol predates bars.

segments.title: Pompeii and Roman roadside inns
segments.summary: The earliest established bars are linked to Pompeii's hot snack bars with wine. Romans built roads with inns and bars for travelers, and bars later spread through pubs and taverns.

segments.title: Shawn's in Athlone and Gassy Jack in Vancouver
segments.summary: Shawn's in Athlone, Ireland is described as possibly the oldest bar in the world, with the town built around it. The hosts then discuss Gassy Jack, who built a bar first in Gastown, Vancouver, and the Globe.

segments.title: Victoria pubs and hotel bars
segments.summary: The hosts mention old Victoria pubs and note that the tradition of bars in hotels continued long after the Roman roads.

segments.title: Bartenders' wealth and the 1832 Pioneer Inn and Tavern law
segments.summary: Bartenders were often wealthy because they owned the bar and made their own booze. In 1832 a US law let people drink in bars without staying in the hotel, and industrial-age immigrants spread bars quickly in cities like New York.

segments.title: Election day drinking and George Washington
segments.summary: Bars were political centers. Candidates swilled voters with bumbo, a rum. George Washington lost his first Virginia Legislature bid, then spent most of his campaign fund on election-day booze and won. Some states later banned election-day drinking; South Carolina and Kentucky still do.

segments.title: Squarespace sponsor read
segments.summary: Sponsor read for Squarespace website builder, with a fourteen-day free trial and offer code.

segments.title: Erasmus Willard and Jerry Thomas
segments.summary: Erasmus Willard, a famed ambidextrous, photographic-memory bartender at New York's City Hotel, is called the first celebrity bartender. Jerry Thomas, the flamboyant hero of the hosts, tended bar with diamonds and rats, served the Blue Blazer, and published The Bartender's Guide in 1862.

segments.title: Temperance movement and Canadian prescription liquor
segments.summary: The temperance movement led to Prohibition. In Canada during prohibition, people obtained booze by doctor's prescription; Ontario issued about 810,000 in one year, a tenth of Canada's population.

segments.title: US Prohibition, speakeasies and women in bars
segments.summary: US Prohibition produced about thirty thousand speakeasies, twice the number of legal bars before it. Bootleg industrial alcohol was poisoned and killed many. Women began going to bars during Prohibition, and Alberta had gender-specific bar laws until the 1980s.

segments.title: World War II, tiki culture and the fern bar era
segments.summary: Returning soldiers shaped pub culture in Canada and tiki culture in the US. In the 1970s, fern bars with tiffany lamps and chemical mixers, such as Henry Africa's and Perry's in San Francisco, dominated, along with sexual revolution-era singles bars.

segments.title: Dale DeGroff and the cocktail revival
segments.summary: Restaurateur asks Dale DeGroff to set up a bar; DeGroff uses Jerry Thomas's book to bring back real ingredients, fresh fruit and craftsmanship, saving the bar.

segments.title: Cocktail origins: punch, sling, sour, daisy, margarita
segments.summary: Drinks evolved from punches and toddies to slings, which Jerry Thomas developed into the Baroque era of cocktails. The rooster cocktail's name and early morning drinks are covered, along with the sour, fizz, daisy and margarita origins.

segments.title: Martini, daiquiri, Tom Collins, mojito and Caesar
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Martini recipes and disputed origins (Martinez, California, Martini and Rossi), the daiquiri's Cuban origin, the Tom Collins hoax, the mojito's pirate-era roots, and the Caesar's origin in Canada.

segments.title: Canadian whiskey, rye and Canadian Club hide-a-case
segments.summary: Canadian whiskey, called rye in Canada, is compared with bourbon. The Congress country-of-origin labeling law led to Canadian Club's name. The 1960s-80s Hide a Case campaign hid whiskey cases around the world.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts wrap up, invite listeners to search for more on bars and share contact channels.
